query: The (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy provides a large caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field operation but has poor integrity and tends to crack. Prior studies on related MM′X materials used epoxy-containing Mn0.98CoGe, obtaining compressive strengths of 152 and 218 MPa at two epoxy contents, and low-melting In composites, obtaining 48 MPa compressive strength and more than eight times the thermal conductivity of epoxy-containing samples under the reported conditions. These routes demonstrated gains in selected strength or heat-transport metrics, but the desired coexistence of robust integrity and high caloric performance remains unresolved. The target should also remain rare-earth-free. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing caloric response? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, quantitative or directional outcomes relative to the unchanged alloy, boundary conditions under applied-field, pressure, temperature, and loading regimes, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive controlled experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Incorporating a minor addition (≈2–3 at.%) of Cu into the (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy will trigger the in situ formation of a fine, dispersed Cu-rich ductile phase and/or refine the grain structure. This secondary phase will act to arrest crack propagation and redistribute stress during field-induced phase transitions, thereby enhancing the alloy’s mechanical integrity without compromising its large magneto– and barocaloric response.
generation.material_initial_state: The (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy in its as-cast/sintered state, which exhibits excellent caloric performance but suffers from poor compressive strength and crack-prone behavior.
generation.intervention: Introduce approximately 2–3 atomic percent Cu into the alloy composition.
generation.conditions: Tested under applied magnetic fields (up to a few Tesla) and pressure fields within the operational barocaloric range, over the temperature interval where the caloric phase transformation is active, and under compressive mechanical loading.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a finely dispersed, ductile Cu-rich second phase and/or grain refinement, which improves stress distribution at the microstructural level.
generation.mechanism: The Cu-rich phase is expected to serve as a crack arrester by absorbing and redistributing local stresses during the phase transformation associated with the caloric effect. This intervention leverages known strategies in phase engineering from related shape memory and magnetocaloric alloys to enhance toughness without impeding the reversible caloric transformation.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Cu-alloyed material will exhibit improved mechanical integrity (targeting an increase in compressive strength to values above 200 MPa and reduced cracking) while retaining its large caloric response (with isothermal entropy change and adiabatic temperature change remaining within the same order of magnitude as the unalloyed system).
generation.baseline: The original (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy, which shows large caloric effects but poor mechanical integrity (cracking and lower compressive strength).
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies under the operational conditions specified: applied magnetic fields (up to a few Tesla), barocaloric pressure limits, the temperature range where the magnetostructural transformation occurs, and under compressive loading conditions representative of service environments. It is assumed that the alloy remains rare-earth–free and that the processing conditions allow for homogeneous Cu distribution.
generation.uncertainty: While similar strategies in related systems support the potential of minor ductile phase additions to enhance toughness, the precise quantitative effects on both mechanical strength and caloric performance in this specific alloy are uncertain. There is a risk that even slight microstructural changes could affect the caloric behavior if the Cu-rich phase is not optimally dispersed.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of samples: one set of the standard (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy and a second set with a 2–3 at.% Cu addition processed under identical conditions. Subject both sets to identical testing under applied magnetic and pressure fields, as well as identical compressive mechanical loading conditions over the temperature range of the caloric phase transformation.
measurements: Crack propagation behavior (using microscopic imaging and fracture analysis)
Caloric performance metrics (isothermal entropy change and adiabatic temperature change under applied fields)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Cu-alloyed samples do not demonstrate a statistically significant improvement in mechanical integrity (e.g., by failing to reach or exceed a compressive strength >200 MPa or showing similar cracking behavior as the baseline) OR if the caloric response degrades significantly compared to the standard alloy, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

frame.system: The (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high‐entropy alloy in its as‐cast/sintered state that exhibits a magneto– and barocaloric phase transformation but suffers from poor mechanical integrity (cracking).
frame.goal: Achieve simultaneous robust structural integrity (e.g., improved compressive strength and crack resistance) and retention of the large caloric response under applied magnetic and pressure fields, while remaining rare‐earth–free.
frame.limitation: The current alloy shows excellent caloric effects but poor mechanical integrity. Prior composite strategies (using epoxy or low-melting In) have improved selected metrics (strength vs. thermal conductivity) yet have not produced the desired coexistence of high mechanical robustness with high caloric performance.
root_cause_cues: has poor integrity and tends to crack
gains in selected strength or heat-transport metrics
desired coexistence of robust integrity and high caloric performance remains unresolved
constraints: Intervention must not sacrifice the high caloric performance
frame.regime: Under the operating conditions of applied magnetic and pressure fields (i.e., the field‐induced caloric regimes) and across the temperature range over which the magnetostructural (or martensitic) transformation is active, as well as under mechanical loading (compressive regimes relevant for strength measurements).
prior_attempts: Use of epoxy-containing Mn0.98CoGe composites, which achieved compressive strengths of 152–218 MPa at two epoxy contents
Low-melting In composites that produced only 48 MPa compressive strength but highly enhanced thermal conductivity (over eight times that of epoxy-containing samples)
frame.hypothesis: A single intervention that could overcome the limitation is minor alloying with a ductile element such as approximately 2–3 at.% Cu. This addition is hypothesized to promote an in situ formation of a finely dispersed, ductile Cu-rich second phase and/or refine the grain structure. Mechanistically, the ductile phase would act as a crack arrester and stress distributor during the field-induced phase transformation, thereby enhancing compressive strength (targeting values >200 MPa) and resistance to cracking, while maintaining the reversible phase transformation responsible for the large caloric effect. The intervention is predicted to yield either no degradation or only a slight improvement in the caloric response magnitude relative to the unchanged alloy, under applied magnetic fields (e.g., up to a few Tesla), pressures (within the barocaloric operational limits), and over the temperature range of the phase transition. Prior evidence from similar alloy systems in shape memory and magnetocaloric materials suggests that minor ductile phase additions can increase toughness without impairing functional phase transformations. A decisive controlled experiment would involve fabricating two sets of samples—one with the standard composition and one with ~2–3 at.% Cu added—subjecting both to identical applied magnetic and pressure fields, and then simultaneously measuring their caloric effects (isothermal entropy change and adiabatic temperature change) and mechanical properties (compressive strength, crack propagation behavior). If the Cu-alloyed samples do not show an improvement in mechanical integrity (e.g., compressive strength) or if the caloric response deteriorates significantly compared to the pure (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy, the hypothesis would be falsified.

decision.trend: Earlier studies in related high‐entropy or multi‐functional alloys have attempted to improve mechanical properties by forming composites or secondary phases. For example, epoxy‐based composites boosted the compressive strength up to 152–218 MPa, whereas low-melting In composites were used to enhance heat transport, albeit with low strength (48 MPa). Separately, work on reinforcing HEA matrices with hard reinforcements (e.g., TiC in PMC8402061 or ceramic reinforcements as in PMC9744852) shows that phase engineering can improve strength, but often the trade-off was on one metric rather than achieving a balanced multifunctional performance. The composite routes, though beneficial in certain performance facets, have not yet provided a route to simultaneously preserve the large caloric response and enhance mechanical robustness.
decision.unsolved: The challenge remains to obtain both a robust mechanical integrity (high compressive strength and crack resistance) and the excellent caloric response of the (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy. Existing composite strategies have improved one metric at the cost of another, and no intervention has yet balanced these competing requirements in a rare-earth–free design.
decision.lever: Introduce a minor (~2–3 at.%) addition of a ductile element such as Cu
decision.why: Based on the trend in tailoring microstructures through phase engineering in high-entropy systems, a small, controlled compositional change is the most plausible next step. An addition of Cu is hypothesized to trigger the in situ formation of a finely dispersed ductile Cu-rich phase and/or to refine the grain structure, thus arresting crack propagation and distributing stress during field-induced phase transitions. This approach follows prior successes in related alloy systems where minor alloying improved toughness without compromising functional transformations. A decisive experiment comparing standard and Cu-alloyed samples under identical magnetic and pressure fields would determine if the mechanical robustness improves (targeting compressive strengths >200 MPa) while retaining the large caloric response.

families.principle: Altering the alloy chemistry to introduce a new element can tune phase stability and induce in situ formation of secondary phases that arrest cracks while preserving the intrinsic caloric phase transformation.
cues_for: poor integrity and tends to crack
desired coexistence of robust integrity and high caloric performance
cues_against: composite routes (epoxy or In) have been tried and they sacrifice one property over the other
families.best_lever: Minor alloying with 2–3 at.% Cu to promote a finely dispersed, ductile Cu-rich secondary phase without altering the caloric phase transformation

families.principle: Heat treatments or combined thermal-mechanical cycles can induce grain refinements and precipitate formation that improve toughness.
cues_for: the possibility of refining grain structure to improve mechanical integrity
cues_against: such treatments could inadvertently alter the magnetostructural transformation essential for the caloric response, and prior attempts have not resolved the coexistence issue
families.best_lever: A controlled post-sintering anneal under pressure designed to refine grains without modifying the transformation temperature range

families.principle: Designing or engineering the microstructural layout (e.g., controlled distribution of phases or grain boundary engineering) can enhance crack resistance while retaining functional properties.
cues_for: the need to arrest crack propagation and distribute stresses during phase transformation
prior evidence showing that finer microstructures can increase toughness
cues_against: the hypothesis favors a direct composition adjustment and microstructure effects arising indirectly from alloying, rather than a separate architectural design process
families.best_lever: Utilizing processing techniques that promote an intrinsic, refined dispersion of a ductile phase within the primary matrix

families.principle: Adjusting the casting, sintering, or synthesis conditions can optimize defect distributions and solidification rates, potentially reducing crack formation.
cues_for: prior studies have focused on composite processing routes
cues_against: the target is a single intervention that does not compromise the intrinsic caloric response, and bulk processing adjustments risk altering phase transformation kinetics
families.best_lever: Optimizing sintering parameters (e.g., hot pressing with controlled cooling) to refine microstructure and reduce internal stress

families.principle: Modifying the surface or interface (through coatings or engineered boundary layers) can mechanically shield critical regions and mitigate cracking.
cues_for: the issue of cracking suggests that protecting vulnerable surfaces might help
cues_against: the intervention requires a single, bulk modification that preserves the caloric effect; surface treatments may not influence the bulk phase transformation and could interfere with field interactions
families.best_lever: Applying a thin, ductile coating that can absorb stress at the surface, though it is less promising given the bulk property requirements
